name: Training-Serving Skew
intent: Understand how a model can score well offline and badly in production because its inputs are computed differently, and how to prevent, detect and fix the gap.
scenario: A fraud model shows excellent accuracy on held-out data, but in production it misses fraud it should catch and flags good customers. No code throws an error, and the model file is the one that was tested.
problem: A model learns from features computed in the training pipeline and is later fed features computed by the serving path. If the two pipelines compute the same feature differently, the model sees inputs in production that it never saw in training. Nothing fails. The predictions are just worse, and the cause is far from the model, which makes the problem hard to find.

howItWorks.title: Two paths compute the same feature
howItWorks.text: Training usually builds features from stored history in batch, in a data warehouse or notebook. Serving computes them for one live request, in a service, often written by another team in another language. Each path is correct on its own terms, and they can still disagree.

howItWorks.title: How the paths drift apart
howItWorks.text: Rounding and time-zone differences, different handling of missing values, a different definition of a window such as the last 7 days, features that are stale by the time they are used, and fields renamed in one path only. Each one changes the numbers the model sees, in a small way that adds up.

howItWorks.title: Leakage is skew in time
howItWorks.text: A training join that uses data from after the moment of prediction, such as an account status as of today for a transaction from last year, makes the model look better offline than it can ever be live. Training rows must use only what was known at their own timestamp: a point-in-time join.

howItWorks.title: It hides
howItWorks.text: There is no error and no crash. Overall metrics move slowly, and averages can look fine while particular segments degrade. The Rules of Machine Learning guide lists measuring training-serving skew as a rule of its own, and advises checking that the training and serving environments give the same score.

howItWorks.title: Detect it by comparing
howItWorks.text: Log the features that the serving path actually used for each prediction. Compare their distributions, and for a sample the exact values, with what the training pipeline would compute for the same entity and time. Replaying real requests through both paths is a strong test, and so is a test of the example-creation code in both.

howItWorks.title: Prevent it with one definition
howItWorks.text: Define each feature once and use the same code or the same store for training and serving. A feature store computes a feature one time and gives it to training as a point-in-time history and to serving as the latest value. Keep monitoring afterwards, since the world and the code both change.

pros: One feature definition removes a whole class of silent errors
Point-in-time correctness makes offline results believable
Logging served features gives a ground truth to compare and to retrain on
Monitoring the gap catches problems before the users do
cons: A shared definition needs agreement between the data and the serving teams, and some tooling
A feature store is one more system to run, and it needs low-latency access for serving
Replaying and comparing at scale takes storage and compute
Some skew is hard to remove, such as features that depend on live state
whenToUse: A model is trained offline and served online with features computed in different systems
Offline metrics and live results disagree and no code error explains it
You are designing the feature pipeline for a new model
whenNotToUse: Do not build a feature store for a single model with a handful of simple features
Do not assume skew is ruled out because both pipelines were tested separately
Do not treat an offline score as the expected live score without checking the inputs
pitfalls: Re-implementing a feature in the serving service from a written description
Joining training data with the latest values instead of the values at each row's timestamp
Filling missing values with different defaults in training and in serving
Checking the average of a feature and missing the segments where the two paths disagree

roles.label: Training pipeline
roles.description: Builds features in batch from history, and produces the model.

roles.label: Serving path
roles.description: Computes the features for one live request and feeds them to the model.

roles.label: Feature definition
roles.description: The one written rule for how a feature is computed. Both paths should use it.

roles.label: Skew monitor
roles.description: Logs served features and compares them with what training would have produced.

sources.title: Rules of Machine Learning: Best Practices for ML Engineering

quiz.question: A fraud model scores very well offline but poorly in production. Training features come from SQL and serving features come from a separate Java service. What is the best first check?
options: Retrain the model with a larger neural network, since offline scores prove that the model is not at fault
Log the features the serving path used and compare them with the training pipeline's values for the same entities
Lower the decision threshold of the model, which fixes any difference between offline and live results
Wait a month, because a model needs time in production before its live scores become comparable
quiz.explanation: The model is the same, so the likely difference is in its inputs. Comparing the served features with what training would have computed shows where the two paths disagree. A bigger model, a different threshold or waiting do not remove a difference between the inputs.

quiz.question: A training set joins each past transaction with the customer's account status as of today. The model looks excellent offline and fails live. What went wrong?
options: The model has too many parameters, so it memorised the status values instead of learning from them
The status field uses the wrong data type, which always causes a large drop in live accuracy
The learning rate was too high, which makes a model look good on training data but not live
Information from after each transaction leaked into training, so the join must be point-in-time
quiz.explanation: Using today's status for old transactions gives the model information that was not known when it had to decide. Live, that information is not available, so performance collapses. A point-in-time join uses each row's status as it was at the row's own timestamp.

quiz.question: What is the best structural way to prevent training-serving skew?
options: Define each feature once, and use the same code or a feature store for both training and serving
Write the feature logic twice, in two languages, so that each path is optimised on its own
Document each feature in a wiki, and ask both teams to follow the description exactly
Test the model only on serving data, and never on the data that was used for training
quiz.explanation: Two implementations are two chances to disagree, and a description is not a guarantee. A single definition, shared or served from a feature store, removes the disagreement at its source. Testing on serving data helps detect the problem, but does not prevent it.
